name: Dhuska
description: A thick deep-fried disc of briefly fermented ground rice, chana dal and urad dal, flavoured with green chilli, ginger and cumin; crisp outside and soft inside. It is considered Jharkhand's most iconic street food and a common breakfast.
how_to_eat: Eat hot with ghugni (black chickpea curry) or aloo curry.
how_to_order: Ask for 'dhuska ghugni' at breakfast stalls and weekly haats.

name: Muri Ghugni
description: Puffed rice (muri) topped with ghugni, a dark, tangy curry of black chickpeas with onion, tomato, cumin and dry spices. It is a cheap, filling everyday snack.
how_to_eat: Eat standing, from a sal-leaf bowl.
how_to_order: Ask for 'muri ghugni' at weekly haats and roadside stalls.

name: Rugra (Putka)
description: A wild monsoon mushroom foraged from around sal tree roots, with an earthy, meaty flavour and dense texture; it cannot be farmed. It is sautéed in mustard oil with onion, garlic, dried red chillies and turmeric.
how_to_eat: Eat the curry with steamed rice.
how_to_order: Look for 'rugra' at local markets during the monsoon and ask for rugra curry at home-style eateries.

name: Chilka Roti
description: A thin, dosa-like pancake of rice flour with chana dal (and sometimes urad dal), cooked on a tawa with little oil. It is made for festivals and special occasions.
how_to_eat: Eat with chana dal chutney, a vegetable curry, or mutton curry.
how_to_order: Mostly home food; ask for 'chilka roti' at Jharkhandi restaurants.

name: Litti Chokha
description: Wheat dough balls stuffed with spiced sattu, roasted over coal, served with chokha of roasted brinjal, potato and tomato. A Bihari influence, it is a filling everyday meal in Jharkhand.
how_to_eat: Dip the litti in ghee and eat with chokha and papad.
how_to_order: Ask for 'litti chokha' at roadside stalls.

name: Maduwa Khassi
description: Smoked mutton cooked with the skin intact, served with rice.
how_to_eat: Eat with rice.
how_to_order: Mostly cooked at home and community feasts.

name: Rohad Haku
description: Sun-dried fish stir-fried in oil with lemon and vinegar.
how_to_eat: Eat as a side with rice.
how_to_order: Mostly home food in tribal households.

name: Bamboo Shoot Sabzi
description: Young forest bamboo shoots cooked as an earthy, slightly tangy vegetable with basic spices. Bamboo shoots are part of the state's staple diet.
how_to_eat: Eat with plain rice.
how_to_order: Ask for 'bamboo shoot sabzi' at local markets or home-style eateries in season.

name: Sanai ke Phool
description: A seasonal dish of sunn hemp (Crotalaria juncea) blossoms with mustard seeds, dried red chillies and turmeric, mildly bitter and grassy. It is tied to Munda and Santhal farming traditions and is also made as a mashed bharta.
how_to_eat: Eat with rice or roti.
how_to_order: Mostly home food when the flowers bloom.

name: Chakod Jhor
description: A thin, sour curry of chakod, a wild forest green, with minimal spicing and sometimes mustard paste; it is also cooked in a red-rice soup. Santhal and Ho households make it in the monsoon and consider it cooling.
how_to_eat: Eat with rice.
how_to_order: Mostly home food in the monsoon.

name: Koinar Saag
description: Leaves of the koinar tree (Bauhinia variegata) cooked as a vegetable, one of many forest greens eaten in Jharkhand.
how_to_eat: Eat with rice and dal.
how_to_order: Look for koinar leaves at village markets in season.

name: Putkal Saag
description: Sautéed leaves of the putkal tree (Ficus geniculata), a seasonal forest green.
how_to_eat: Eat with rice.
how_to_order: Mostly home food in season.

name: Moonj Ada
description: A spicy dal cooked slowly over low heat with lemon and chilli.
how_to_eat: Eat with rice.
how_to_order: Mostly home food.

name: Red Ant Chutney
description: A tribal chutney of mashed red weaver ants and their eggs, with a distinct taste. It is eaten by tribal communities in Jharkhand and neighbouring states.
how_to_eat: Eat a small amount as a relish with rice.
how_to_order: Look for it at tribal village haats; it is rarely on restaurant menus.

name: Jirhul Flower Pakoda
description: Palash (flame-of-the-forest) flowers dipped in spiced gram-flour batter and fried, faintly floral and slightly bitter. It is made mainly around spring festivals such as Sarhul, by Munda and Oraon communities for whom the tree is sacred.
how_to_eat: Eat hot as a snack.
how_to_order: Mostly home-made in spring.

name: Dal Pitha
description: A rice-flour dumpling stuffed with chana dal seasoned with ginger, garlic and mustard, steamed in banana or sal leaf. Munda and Oraon households make it in winter.
how_to_eat: Eat warm with green chutney or a mustard dip.
how_to_order: Mostly home-made in winter and at festivals.

name: Thekua
description: A crisp fried sweet of wheat flour, fennel and jaggery or sugar cooked in ghee, with a long shelf life. It is offered as prasad at Chhath Puja and eaten as an evening snack.
how_to_eat: Eat with tea.
how_to_order: Ask for 'thekua' at sweet shops around Chhath.

name: Malpua
description: A fried, sweetened pancake synonymous with Holi in Jharkhand; the local version is thicker and less sugary, only lightly dipped in syrup.
how_to_eat: Eat warm.
how_to_order: Mostly home-made on the eve of Holi; also at sweet shops.

name: Arsa Roti
description: A fried sweet flatbread of rice flour and jaggery, crisp outside and chewy inside, that keeps for several days. It is made for festivals and weddings.
how_to_eat: Eat as a sweet snack.
how_to_order: Mostly home-made for festivals and weddings.

name: Tilkut (Til Barfi)
description: A winter sweet of pounded sesame seeds bound with jaggery or melted sugar. It is made mainly for Makar Sankranti and sold in markets during winter.
how_to_eat: Eat as a snack in winter.
how_to_order: Ask for 'tilkut' at sweet shops and markets in winter.

name: Dumbu
description: A rice-based dessert of Jharkhand.
how_to_order: Mostly home-made.

name: Mitha Khaja
description: A sweet made in nearly every household and exchanged with friends and relatives in the festive season; it is synonymous with Diwali in the state.
how_to_eat: Eat as a festive sweet.
how_to_order: Ask for 'khaja' at sweet shops around Diwali.

name: Deoghar Kesar Peda
description: Saffron-flavoured milk peda sold outside the Baba Baidyanath temple in Deoghar, a speciality of a decades-old sweet shop there.
how_to_eat: Eat as prasad after the temple visit.
how_to_order: Ask for 'kesar peda' at sweet shops outside the Deoghar temple.

name: Handia
description: A mild, cloudy, slightly sour rice beer made by fermenting boiled rice with ranu tablets, dried cakes of 20-25 wild herbs and roots, for about a week. Munda, Santhal and Ho communities offer it to guests and serve it at festivals, weddings and rites.
how_to_eat: Drink from a leaf cup or clay pot, as offered.
how_to_order: Found at village haats and festivals rather than shops; accept it when offered as hospitality.

name: Mahua Daru
description: A liquor distilled from the flowers of the mahua tree (Madhuca longifolia).
how_to_eat: Drink in small amounts; it is much stronger than handia.
how_to_order: Found at village haats rather than shops.
